justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three horizons, starting near 137.5 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 139.0 at one month. This gentle slope assumes that whatever asset or indicator I was forecasting was trading in a relatively stable regime with a slight positive bias, consistent with recent momentum or a mild mean-reversion toward a slightly higher equilibrium level. The one-day estimate is anchored most heavily to the last observed price or value, with very little assumed drift, while the one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a small expected trend component that compounds modestly over time. In the absence of specific fundamental catalysts, this kind of near-flat projection with marginal upside is a common baseline when conditions appear calm and directional signals are ambiguous.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 6 points, consistent with typical short-term volatility in a relatively stable market environment. By one week, the interval widens to 12 points, and at one month it reaches 24 points, roughly doubling at each step. These widths were calibrated to reflect realized or implied volatility levels, accounting for the fact that small daily fluctuations accumulate and can produce meaningfully different outcomes over weeks. I also factored in some asymmetry risk and fat-tail behavior typical of financial markets, though the symmetric presentation of the intervals suggests I did not strongly lean toward skew in either direction at the time.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a better-than-expected economic data release, an unexpected policy shift, or a significant demand shock — could drive values well above 151 at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a risk-off episode, a liquidity crunch, geopolitical escalation, or a negative earnings or macro surprise could push values below 127. Tail events by definition are underweighted in any confidence interval, and the one-month window is long enough that multiple compounding shocks could occur.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume a relatively stationary volatility environment. If realized volatility were to spike — as it often does during periods of market stress — the actual distribution of outcomes would have much fatter tails than my stated 90% intervals imply. Regime changes, such as a sudden shift in central bank policy or a structural break in market conditions, represent the most significant source of outside-interval risk. These are precisely the scenarios that historical volatility estimates tend to underweight, which is a known limitation of any forecast grounded in recent data.
